name: Metadata and Ontologies
title: Metadata and Ontologies
answer: Metadata is structured description of research objects: datasets, models, papers, software, and samples. It records who, what, when, where, how, rights, provenance, and identifiers. Ontologies go further, defining classes, properties, relationships, and rules for a domain so that terms from different sources can be mapped and queried. In a library of 135 research papers, metadata is the layer that makes each item findable, citable, and reusable. For AI research, metadata also covers model cards, dataset sheets, evaluation claims, and links to original papers.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Metadata is structured description of research objects: datasets, models, papers, software, and samples. It records who, what, when, where, how, rights, provenance, and identifiers. Ontologies go further, defining classes, properties, relationships, and rules for a domain so that terms from different sources can be mapped and queried. In a library of 135 research papers, metadata is the layer that makes each item findable, citable, and reusable. For AI research, metadata also covers model cards, dataset sheets, evaluation claims, and links to original papers.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Metadata and ontologies run on repository platforms, catalog systems, graph databases, and triple stores that speak RDF and SPARQL. Common vocabularies include Dublin Core, DataCite, schema.org, SKOS, and OWL, often serialized as JSON-LD, Turtle, or XML. Persistent identifiers such as DOI, ORCID, and ROR anchor people, organizations, and objects. APIs, harvesters like OAI-PMH, and schema registries let repositories exchange records. Ontology editors such as Protégé and version control systems support authoring and maintenance.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work starts with domain scoping and reuse: check existing vocabularies before defining new terms. Curators and researchers elicit concepts, write definitions, assign stable identifiers, and record relationships. They map local terms to shared ontologies, validate with reasoners and validation rules, and test queries against real repository data. Metadata extraction from papers and datasets can be manual, semi-automated, or model-assisted, with human review. Versioning, deprecation notes, and change logs keep the ontology usable over time.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk: metadata can expose personal data, unpublished findings, or sensitive locations, so access controls and licenses matter. Provenance records who created or changed a term, from which source, and under what license. Ontology reuse raises attribution and compatibility risks, especially when licenses conflict or terms drift. Repositories need clear policies for corrections, takedowns, and persistent identifiers. Ethical review and data protection rules apply to metadata as much as to the data itself.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going: more automated metadata generation from papers, code, and models, with human curation. Ontologies are moving toward modular, versioned, machine-readable profiles that align across domains. FAIR principles and open science policies push repositories to expose richer provenance and citation links. AI systems increasingly consume metadata and ontologies for retrieval, reasoning, and reproducibility checks. The hard part remains maintenance, community agreement, and keeping terms meaningful as fields change.
